title: Dad left us a neglected shop lot. Should we sell it, renovate it or rent it out?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #243 | INHERIT MY DAD'S MISTAKE
excerpt: A family inherited a paid-off shop lot bought above market in 2005, empty for years with RM50,000 in unpaid taxes. Sean says get three numbers, then sell unless they still believe in the area.

qa.asker: Mr L, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: Mr L, 30, lost his father just before Chinese New Year. His father's will left his mother a fully paid double-storey shop lot in Bukit Beruntung, bought in 2005 well above market price and left vacant and unattended; an agent suggests about RM1,000 a month in rent. It carries about RM50,000 in unpaid quit rent and assessment, and the family's only other fund is a RM100,000 life insurance payout meant to support his mother, who turns 60 this year.
qa.question: Should the family sell it as it is, renovate and sell, or renovate and rent it out for his mother's income?
qa.quote: Do you still believe in this location?
qa.answer: Find three numbers first: the renovation cost, the price as it stands and the price once made good. Unless the family still believes in the area, selling is the obvious choice: a sale of around RM500,000 kept in fixed deposit would beat RM1,000 a month in rent, and what their father paid no longer matters.

reasons.title: His purchase price isn't their loss
reasons.body: The loan is fully paid, so whatever it sells for is money in the family's hands. Recent listings nearby averaged about RM600,000, so Sean assumes about RM500,000 given its condition.

reasons.title: RM80,000 for RM1,000 a month doesn't add up
reasons.body: Clearing the RM50,000 in arrears and perhaps RM20,000 to RM30,000 of work, to earn RM1,000 a month, isn't justified for a family already stretched. Rents quoted nearby ranged from RM900 to RM5,000, so check with several agents.

reasons.title: Shop lots need little work
reasons.body: A commercial unit only has to be restored to its original state: grilles, shutters, windows, wiring, water and a sound roof. Tenants fit it out for their business, so a cheaper or even DIY job may be enough.

reasons.title: Refinancing needs a qualifying borrower
reasons.body: Keeping it and refinancing to fund the work only works if the new owner has enough income for the bank's debt service ratio. A paid-off property alone won't get a loan.

actions: Get quotes for restoring the unit to working order, and consider doing simple work yourselves.
Ask several agents for the price as it is and the price once made good, and compare rents from more than one source.
If renovating to sell gains much more than it costs and you can fund it, do it; if not, sell as it is and expect buyers to negotiate.
Keep the unit only if the family still believes the area will develop, and check who would qualify for any refinancing.
If you invest in property yourself, keep three to six months' emergency fund and enough MRTA, MLTA or life cover that loans never pass to your family as debts.
qa.caveat: Sean couldn't judge the damage or renovation cost from the email, so the figures are rough. If the family believes the area will take off again, holding on can be reasonable, but only with the arrears cleared and someone able to manage the unit.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #243. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Market prices and rents are rough figures Sean read from listings during the episode in March 2024. The episode was sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean works with.
